subject: chemistry-hl
about: Original practice questions written for NevaIB from the IB guide's syllabus understandings and the school's unit order. Not IB past-paper questions, not publisher material and not IB markschemes: the marking points are written for self-marking. Organisms, experiments and data in data-response items are invented for practice.

choices: Heat is released to the surroundings, so ΔH is negative
Heat is absorbed from the surroundings, so ΔH is positive
Heat is released to the surroundings, so ΔH is positive
The temperature of the surroundings falls as bonds form
items.note: Exothermic: system loses energy, surroundings warm up, ΔH < 0. Sign is about the system, not the surroundings.
Melting needs energy to overcome intermolecular forces. Combustion, neutralisation and condensation release energy.

items.stem: Which expression gives the heat energy absorbed by water in a calorimeter?
items.note: q = mcΔT with m the mass of water (g), c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ and ΔT the temperature change (K or °C).

items.stem: In an energy profile for an exothermic reaction:
choices: The products are lower in energy than the reactants
The reactants are lower in energy than the products
The transition state is lower than the products
items.note: ΔH = H(products) − H(reactants) is negative. Activation energy is always positive — the peak is above both.

items.stem: Standard conditions for enthalpy changes in the IB data booklet are:
choices: 100 kPa and a stated temperature, usually 298 K
items.note: Standard state = 100 kPa, solutions 1 mol dm⁻³, usually quoted at 298 K. STP (273 K) is for gas volumes.

items.stem: 50.0 cm³ of acid is mixed with 50.0 cm³ of alkali; the temperature rises by 6.5 °C. Assuming the solution behaves like water (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹), the heat released is:
items.note: m = 100.0 g (total volume), q = 100.0 × 4.18 × 6.5 = 2717 J = 2.72 kJ. Using only 50 g gives 1.36 kJ.

items.stem: 0.0250 mol of water forms when 1.36 kJ is released in a neutralisation. What is ΔH for the reaction per mole of water?
items.note: ΔH = −q ÷ n = −1.36 ÷ 0.0250 = −54.4 kJ mol⁻¹. Add the negative sign because heat was released.

items.stem: In a simple coffee-cup calorimetry experiment, the main reason the measured ΔH is less exothermic than the literature value is:
choices: The mass of solution is too large
Heat is lost to the surroundings
items.note: Heat loss means the measured ΔT is too small, so |ΔH| is too small. Use a lid, insulation and extrapolate the cooling curve.

items.stem: A temperature–time graph is plotted, and the cooling line after mixing is extrapolated back to the time of mixing. The purpose is to:
choices: Find the rate of the reaction from the gradient of the line
Find the initial temperature of the two solutions
Estimate the maximum temperature rise as if no heat had been lost
Remove the random error caused by the thermometer
items.note: Extrapolation compensates for heat lost while the reaction was happening, giving a better ΔT.

items.stem: 0.460 g of ethanol (M = 46.08) is burned and heats 100.0 g of water by 25.0 K. What is the experimental enthalpy of combustion?
The same neutralisation is repeated with double the volumes of both solutions at the same concentrations. Compared with the first experiment:
choices: ΔT doubles and ΔH per mole doubles
ΔT halves and ΔH per mole is the same
ΔT doubles and ΔH per mole is the same
ΔT is the same and ΔH per mole is the same
items.note: Twice the moles release twice the heat, but into twice the mass of water, so ΔT is unchanged. ΔH per mole is a fixed property of the reaction.

items.stem: Sketch and label an energy profile for an endothermic reaction. Include ΔH and the activation energy.
markscheme: Activation energy shown from reactants to the peak (1)
ΔH shown as the difference between reactants and products, positive/upward arrow (1)
items.tactic: Profiles: axes labelled (energy / reaction progress), arrows start at the reactant line.

items.stem: Explain why the temperature rises in an exothermic reaction even though the energy of the system decreases.
markscheme: Energy released when bonds form is greater than energy needed to break bonds (1)
This energy is transferred to the surroundings (water/solution), so its temperature rises (1)
items.tactic: Keep system and surroundings separate in your answer.

items.stem: Suggest two improvements to a calorimetry experiment measuring the enthalpy of combustion of a fuel, and explain how each makes the result more accurate.
markscheme: reduces heat lost to the air, so ΔT is closer to the true value (1)
Use a copper (better conducting) calorimeter close to the flame / insulate the sides (1)
more of the heat is transferred to the water (1)
Weigh the burner with its cap on to stop evaporation of the fuel (1)
mass of fuel burned is not overestimated (1)
items.tactic: Each improvement needs a "how it helps" link — two marks per improvement.

items.stem:
(Invented data for practice.) A student found the enthalpy of combustion of an invented liquid fuel, M = 74.12 g mol⁻¹. Mass of burner before 52.384 g, after 51.890 g; water 150.0 g; initial temperature 19.5 °C; maximum 35.8 °C.
(a) Calculate the heat absorbed by the water. (b) Calculate ΔH of combustion in kJ mol⁻¹. (c) The literature value is −2670 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the percentage error and state the main source.
markscheme: Heat lost to the surroundings (or incomplete combustion) (1)
items.tactic: Unfamiliar context: find the syllabus idea being tested, quote the data (with units) when you describe a trend, then explain it with that idea. One marking point per linked step.
